utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-99-36-R77, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin concerning allegations against Milka Maglov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would both parties make their appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Brenda J. Hollis. I appear as Amicus Curiae Prosecutor by direction of the Trial Chamber originally seized of this matter. I was appointed Amicus Curiae Prosecutor by decision dated 30 October, 2004 -- 2003. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hollis. For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, my name is J. Cooper. I appear as pro bono counsel for Mrs. Maglov. I'm joined by Professor Peter Murphy, co-counsel, and Virginia Lindsay who is our senior legal consultant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a Pre-Trial Conference being held pursuant to Rule 73 bis to discuss various matters prior to the commencement of trial. I shall briefly lay out the procedural history of the case. This case arose out of an alleged contempt by Ms. Milka Maglov in her capacity as a member of the Defence team for Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, and the case was initially assigned to the Trial Chamber II, the Chamber hearing that trial against Mr. Brdjanin. In the same Chamber, a contempt trial against Ms. Maglov commenced on 16th February of 2004, and upon completion of the Prosecution's case after four days' hearing, the proceedings were adjourned to allow the Trial Chamber to determine a 98 bis motion. Thereafter, the proceedings was scheduled to resume on 20th of July, 2004. However, a continuance based upon medical reasons was granted. In the meantime, following the issuance of the judgement in the case against Mr. Brdjanin and the completion of the mandate of the two ad litem Judges, the composition of the Trial Chamber was dissolved and, thereafter, on 22nd of September, the present President assigned this case to this Chamber. Having briefly said the procedural history of the case, I now turn to the issues in relation to this Pre-Trial Conference. The first and foremost important issue will be whether this trial should be a trial de novo or it should be a continuation of the prior proceedings. This Chamber is of the view that the continuation of the prior proceedings would only be possible when both parties - the Defence in particular - would agree to it. However, it has been brought to the Chamber's attention by the Senior Legal Officer, who held the 65 ter Conference, that the Defence is opposed to the continuation of prior proceedings. In addition, on the part of the Amicus Curiae Prosecutor, we've also been informed that should there be a trial de novo, there would be some difficulty on the part of the Prosecutor in calling the witnesses again for testimony. So shall we hear from the parties on this matter first. Who should begin first? Yes, Mrs. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would like to begin on the assumption that the proceedings would be de novo proceedings. Although I believe there is an argument to be made for a continuation, I believe that in an abundance of caution, de novo proceedings would be the better approach. Given that there were to be de novo proceedings, then I as the Amicus Curiae Prosecutor would request the Chamber in fact not to proceed with this as a criminal matter. I would request that this Trial Chamber would instead vacate the orders of the prior Trial Chamber which moved this matter forward as a criminal matter. And I believe, Your Honour, that those orders were dated initially the 15th of April, 2003, where the Trial Chamber ordered that they determined that this matter would proceed on two original charges as a criminal matter. Then on the 6th of February, 2004, the original Trial Chamber approved the amended allegations to move forward as a criminal matter. Were I the Prosecutor in the normal course of proceedings before this Tribunal, I would at this point be making a motion pursuant to Rule of Procedure And Evidence 51(A)(iii) and Rule 73(A) that the indictment be withdrawn. Since these charges are before you not in the normal procedure before this Tribunal, I am making the request instead that you vacate the two prior orders and that this matter be dealt with administratively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, if you could elaborate a bit more on the reasons why this should not be continued on the basis of criminal procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, in a proceeding de novo, the Prosecution of course would be required to put its case on once again. The three primary fact witnesses to these allegations were extremely reluctant to come forward during the last hearing. In particular, the alleged victim referred to as "Witness" was extremely concerned about coming forward both for security reasons and for privacy reasons. This witness had been victimised and traumatised by events during the conflict in Bosnia, had encountered precarious security conditions after the conflict in Bosnia, and had been traumatised by events that occurred that surround these allegations regardless of how respondent's might be characterised. This person was extremely reluctant to come forward, and at the conclusion of testimony indicated a wish that there be no further involvement on the part of this witness in any of these proceedings. In addition to that, two other important fact witnesses were also reluctant. One of them, again for security reasons, dealing with a fear that both personal and professional adverse consequences could flow from that person's appearance here; and the third person was reluctant because of treatment that person had endured during the conflict and because of very strongly felt privacy concerns about coming forward. Given these positions and the fact that despite these grave concerns all three persons came forward and testified, I would suggest to you that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to require so reluctant a group of witness who have already come forward to once again come forward despite their concerns. And, Your Honours, this is the basis upon which I would ask you to take the action that I have requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hollis. What would you say to that on the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're very grateful to Ms. Hollis for her submissions, and we very respectfully support her submissions. We do agree that it would be appropriate for any trial to operate de novo, and we say that bearing in mind our acquaintanceship with the proceedings thus far. In earlier pleadings, which I don't rehearse here, the Defence for Ms. Maglov had set out very extensively what they considered to have been shortcomings in those proceedings. Ms. Maglov herself was not represented by counsel, and she conducted cross-examination herself. In our submission, there could be no substitute for this Trial Chamber proceeding with this matter de novo, there being no substitute for the Trial Chamber itself being able to see the witnesses, to see their demeanour, and to raise its own questions as well as having the assistance of questions raised on Mrs. Maglov's behalf by counsel. So for those reasons, in relation to the first point, we respectfully do agree that the only fair, fully fair procedure to operate now and henceforth, if a trial were to proceed, would be a trial de novo. Having said that, we hear Ms. Hollis's submissions in relation to the witness and indeed all of the witnesses. Those are plainly matters in which the Amicus Prosecutor must look with great care and indeed so must the Trial Chamber. Those are matters about which I myself don't wish to say anything further. We support the application which is effectively being made to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cooper. Ms. Hollis, your submission to withdraw the indictment actually means that a request to vacate the order on the part of the Trial Chamber, and if you could help me, what order it is to be vacated. Was it -- is it the order of the 6th of February of this year, or which order the commencement of the contempt trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In my submission, there would really be two orders that were involved. The order which originally moved this matter forward as a criminal matter, and I believe as I indicated the date of that order was 15 April 2003. That was the order that moved this matter forward on the two original allegations. I believe secondarily the order of 6 February 2004 would also be vacated, and that was the order, I believe, that approved the requested amendments to those allegations and moved the proceeding forward based on those amended allegations. So in my submission, it would be necessary to vacate both those orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hollis. The Chamber will consult on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi will put some questions to Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Mrs. Hollis, I listened with great interest to your explanations about the reasons why the witness, who is also a victim, is reluctant to come and testify, but I would like you to clarify something for me. I would like to have your impression. Did you feel that his position not to come back to testify before the honourable Tribunal, did you feel that it was because he had relived or thought about the fear he experienced during -- with the visit that -- when Mrs. Maglov went to visit him? So in other words, did you think that he thought back, he thought of all these -- the fear he experienced at that time, the intimidation? Because at the time, if I understand correctly, at the specific time he didn't feel that it was a matter of intimidation, but only afterwards, when he thought about it later on. That's when, later. That's when he came to the conclusion that maybe there was an attempt at intimidation by Mrs. Maglov. So I'd like to have your personal opinion about that matter, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For this explanation, could we go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in public session. The Amicus Curiae Prosecutor has made an oral motion to this Trial Chamber to vacate the order of Trial Chamber II, dated 15th of April, 2003, and 6th of February, 2004, which ordered to prosecute Ms. Maglov for the contempt charges. In view of the submission by the Amicus Curiae Prosecutor and lack of opposition from the Defence or, rather, its consent, and considering the procedural history of this case and all circumstances surrounding this case, the Chamber hereby grants the motion and vacates the orders. These proceedings are hereby terminated, and this hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Court, we appreciate your timely ruling on this request. At the same time, I would like for the record, at least, to deal with two other issues that arise from the conduct in question here, and I have spoken with the Defence about these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the first issue is what further action might be taken administratively regarding this matter, and in that regard, Your Honour, and I believe in substance, the Defence would not oppose this, the first thing the Prosecution would ask, would like to put on the record is that the Registry consider with great care any future applications by this respondent to appear before this Tribunal in any capacity, taking into consideration the circumstances surrounding her removal as co-counsel in the Brdjanin case as well as the circumstances surrounding these allegations. That would be the first submission. The second submission is that in view of the Amicus Prosecutor, these events raise grave concerns regarding an essential matter, and perhaps there is need for guidance or clarification by some appropriate body at the ICTY regarding this matter, and that is to say regardless of how one were to characterise the conduct of the respondent, it appears to the Amicus Prosecutor that her conduct brings into question what guidance exists or what standard should exist to guide both parties to these proceedings or any proceedings as to how they can initiate contact with persons who may have relevant information in a way that would protect that person's security and privacy concerns. In that regard in relation to this matter, the Prosecution would suggest that one thing, one obligation the parties would have would be to familiarise themselves with materials they had been given, which might make them aware of persons, circumstances and potential security and privacy concerns. In particular, I speak to the disclosure materials that had been made available to the Defence, and according to evidence in the trial had been made available to this respondent, but for a variety reasons, materials which this respondent had not fully familiarised herself. So an issue would be what fundamental procedures should the parties take that their contacts with people do not jeopardise those people or traumatise them, and I suggest this is a matter that should be considered by the appropriate body within the Tribunal and that input from both the Office of the Prosecutor and the Defence bar as well as the Victim and Witnesses Unit should be sought and that some sort of guidance should be provided so that perhaps we could avoid this kind of conduct in the future. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hollis. Yes, Mr. Cooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I address you in relation to those matters that have been raised. In essence, Ms. Hollis makes two submissions to Your Honours. One is a matter of practice and the second is a matter of policy. As to the matter of practice, may I say that we have no objection at all to the form of words that has been proposed by Ms. Hollis in relation to any future application by our client to come onto the Rule 45 list of counsel. Plainly any application will be looked at with the Registrar with great care, and this will be no different. In that context, I should say that pursuant to this Trial Chamber's order, these proceedings will have resolved without an adjudication on the facts, and we make clear that Mrs. Maglov has at no stage made any admission, and she makes no admission of criminal conduct on her part whatsoever. The other matter that I should raise in relation to practice is that it is right that Mrs. Maglov has taken every possible opportunity within these proceedings to express in the clearest terms her own regret if her conduct had inadvertently caused discomfort for Witness W, and on her behalf, I have no hesitation at all in these proceedings of repeating the regret that she herself has expressed. As to policy matters, I'm going to ask Professor Murphy to address those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, as regards Ms. Hollis's submissions about the need for clarity and guidance, we would wish to be associated with those observations. This case has caused a great deal of anxiety not just for Mrs. Maglov but I think it right to say for the Defence bar as a whole, because it raised the question of what Defence counsel could or could not properly do in order to approach and interview a witness. Your Honours will be aware that there are two decisions of the Appeals Chamber in which it is suggested that it is the duty of Defence counsel to approach and interview witnesses as may be necessary without any restrictions. However, clearly that has to be read in the light of the matters affecting privacy to which Ms. Hollis has alluded, and we feel, Your Honour, that this may be an appropriate matter for the Rules Committee at some point to look at with the input of the Office of the Prosecutor, the Defence bar, and Chambers, of course, and also the Victims and Witness Unit. So to that extent, Your Honour, both we and Mrs. Maglov support the -- any efforts that may be made to bring some clarity and guidance to that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that timely and appropriate observation from both parties. Those having been put on record, I don't think there's anything we can deal with right now. So this hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: at 3.38 p.m.
